rv.q: I was entertained, and heard some great language spoken by legends of my time.

Uneven – if not so much as Gold's 2019. King Lear with Glenda Jackson – and peppered with choices both curious and captivating, this iteration of The Scottish Play nearly holds up to the unavoidable hype of its starry cast.
It’s a production that makes you think, but it did not make me feel.

Mr. Craig brings a compelling physical presence to the role, but his interpretation lacks the psychological depth that would make Macbeth's transformation from noble warrior to murderous tyrant truly riveting.
Still, this swift, savvy Macbeth never winds its charm too tightly; only rarely does it feel unearthly.
Yet, despite the charms and potions, there’s not so much magic here.
Language and character yield pride of place to stylishness; a lone jolt of human emotion comes in the very final scene.
But this relentlessly analytical production, directed by Sam Gold, takes even that last quality apart, offering not so much “Macbeth” as a private inquest into it.
It’s a grizzly and unearned grasp for thrills from a production without a cohesive life force of its own.
Gold’s production simply lacks narrative drive. You cannot get fully invested in an evening spent pondering Macbeth’s narrative psyche if you don’t comprehend the world.
Under all the fog (and there is a lot of it), there isn't much substance in this production, which clearly prioritizes an aesthetic and a mood over acting, coherence and Shakespeare's text.

Nevertheless, their talent cannot redeem this overwrought, underacted Skyfail.
In retrospect, that seems appropriate, since this is far more Sam Gold’s Macbeth than the Bard’s.
This is not a grand Macbeth — the staging is too sparse and self-aware, almost tossed-off (or at least determined to give that impression), for that.
These opening and final vistas are not as written by Shakespeare, and the closing one in particular feels bizarre and hokey considering what has just preceded it.
In the end, this Macbeth is a star-enhanced hodgepodge.
Gold’s production underplays everyone’s emotions to the point of nothingness.
The staging sometimes feels like an acting exercise conducted during a rehearsal.
Fine actors like Daniel Craig and Ruth Negga who have demonstrated their top-flight acting chops on stage elsewhere have not been aided by the bizarre direction.
Whatever his rationale, Gold likes to bring a downtown, experimental theater perspective to Broadway, where, really, it simply does not work, at least not with this production of Macbeth.

A curious choice, considering the dramaturgical note in the program.
The same can be said, in fact, for the entire cast, whose performances, even when externally passionate, are full of sound and fury, signifying nothing.
Mr. Craig and Ms. Negga both offer clearly articulated but superficial performances.
Classic works don’t need the modern-dress approach that nowadays is a shabby cliché.

It’s an experience for all the senses from the moment you step into the theatre.
It was actually disconcerting and diminished the tragic elements of the play about a power-hungry man and the destruction his ambitions create.
I can't imagine what someone who's never seen or read the play could possibly get here, except an excuse to catch up on their sleep.

cn.t: Sam Gold's stripped-down "Macbeth" starring Daniel Craig and Ruth Negga draws largely negative reviews for its gimmicky staging and unclear vision, though the leads earn praise for their performances in an otherwise pretentious, uninvolving production.

sg.ra: Longacre's proscenium is narrow (35ft wide, 34'10" high) and the house is shallow, so Row D sits very close without neck-craning; Center Orchestra rows D-L fall inside the mezzanine overhang line (which starts around Row H) but the overhang is shallow enough that top-of-stage cut-off is not reported here, unlike deeper houses.

Longacre is a small-to-mid house (1,077 seats) so 'rear' orchestra is still close by Broadway standards; rows L-N sit behind the mezzanine overhang line (starts ~H) which trims a small slice of upper stage but preserves intimacy and drops the price noticeably versus premium D-K.

Longacre's mezzanine is 'not too high' per SeatPlan - the overhang from the balcony only starts at Row B, so Row A gets a clean head-on elevated view, and unusually generous front-row legroom is a Longacre-specific quirk called out on BroadwayWorld.

Rows D-E sit under the balcony overhang (starts Row B) but Longacre's balcony is small (249 seats, 7 rows) so the overhang depth is modest; sources consistently flag D-E as the honest middle-ground for elevated sightlines before rows F-J start feeling far from the stage.

Longacre's mezzanine rake flattens toward the back per SeatPlan ('the rake may also be slightly too shallow if a taller patron is sitting in front'), and rows F-J are explicitly called out as 'problematic' and 'not the best on account of their considerable distance from the stage' - the small house becomes a disadvantage here since the balcony takes over the better upper-level views.

Longacre-specific quirk: the front balcony rail sits high enough that multiple TripAdvisor reviewers at 5'5" and 5'7" had to lean over the bar the whole show (Macbeth 2022, Swept Away-era 2025), so Row B beats Row A for most patrons - the opposite of the usual 'front row is always best' advice. Also avoid the four structural pillars between rows B and C on the center aisles.

sg.vl: Skip for any show with detail
sg.ra: Longacre's balcony is the oldest-school part of the house - a 1913 Henry B. Herts design with four structural pillars between B-C and a steep rake that gets sound-dead at the back; SeatPlan explicitly warns 'sound quality may be inferior toward the rear' and rows D-G compound distance + pillar risk + tight legroom.
